question:
A data platform team proposes one "super-agent". This single loop does agentic RAG over documents. It does agentic search over the web. It does agentic analytics over the warehouse. All parts share one memory. Two teams own the pieces.

The search team owns retrieval quality. The analytics team owns SQL correctness. The pilot's failures are hard to attribute. Nobody can tell the source of a bad answer.

Constraint: every failure must be attributable to an owner, and each team must be able to eval and ship its piece independently.

Which two changes satisfy the constraint? (Select two)

choices.A: Decompose into three bounded agents (RAG, search, analytics) with explicit input/output contracts, coordinated by a thin orchestrator; each team owns its agent and its eval set.
choices.B: Give the super-agent three labeled memory sections so failures are easier to discuss.
choices.C: Require each team to review the super-agent's full prompt before every release.
choices.D: Version each agent's contract separately and gate releases on that agent's own eval suite, so one team's change cannot silently break another's piece.

explanation:
Why A, D is correct: Bounded agents with contracts make ownership real. Failures stay with the agent. This agent violated its contract (A). Per-agent versioning and eval gates let teams ship independently. This stops cross-team breakage (D). The orchestrator stays thin.

It cannot become a second super-agent.

B is wrong. Labeled memory sections do not create ownership. They do not create independent evaluations. Attribution stays a matter of opinion.

C is wrong. Joint prompt review couples the teams on every release. This is the opposite of independent shipping.

question:
A company builds onboarding Q&A over a 40,000-token policy manual. The first version pastes the entire manual into every request. Token bills are high, and answer quality is actually dropping: the model misses details buried in the middle of the manual.

Constraint: cut cost per question while improving answer accuracy on specific policy details.

What is the right fix?

choices.A: Retrieve only the relevant sections: embed the manual once, fetch the top chunks per question, and put those in context instead of the whole manual.
choices.B: Paste the manual twice so the model sees the middle sections again.
choices.C: Lower the temperature to make answers more precise.
choices.D: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the whole manual fits more comfortably.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Retrieval replaces context stuffing with relevant context. The model sees the sections that matter. It does not see 40,000 tokens of noise. This improves cost and the lost-in-the-middle accuracy problem.
D is wrong. A bigger window does not fix the lost-in-the-middle effect. It does not fix the per-request cost of stuffing the manual. The failure is architectural.
B is wrong. Duplicating the manual doubles the cost. It adds no new information.
C is wrong. Temperature controls randomness. It does not control if the model can find a detail in 40,000 tokens.

question:
An urgent-care network builds a triage classifier. The network labels incoming messages. The network labels messages as routine, urgent, or emergency. A mislabeled emergency can delay care. The vendor recommends pinning the cheapest model. The vendor says "classification is easy and all models score within a point on benchmarks."

Constraint: patient safety dominates; a missed emergency outweighs any cost saving.

How should the architect choose the model?

choices.A: Use the cheapest model but add ten few-shot examples to close the gap.
choices.B: Use the cheapest model for routine messages and skip classification for the rest.
choices.C: Take the cheapest model, since benchmarks show near-parity.
choices.D: Evaluate candidate models on a triage-specific eval set. Weight the eval set by consequence. Missed emergencies cost more than false alarms. Pick the cheapest model that clears the safety bar. Do not pick the cheapest overall model.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Consequence of error must drive model selection. Price must not drive model selection. A consequence-weighted evaluation measures the constraint. This includes missed emergencies. "Cheapest that clears the bar" keeps cost discipline. It does not sacrifice safety.
C is wrong. Generic benchmarks do not measure triage errors. Near-parity on average hides the rare catastrophic misses. The constraint cares about these misses.
A is wrong. Few-shot examples cannot fix the specific failure mode. This includes missed emergencies. This is true without the consequence-weighted evaluation. It is hope, not evidence.
B is wrong. Skipping classification abandons the task for the hardest messages. Triage matters most for these messages.

question:
A team puts task instructions and five few-shot examples after the user message in the prompt. On short inputs the format is perfect. On long customer emails the model suddenly stops following the format, and the team finds the examples were cut off.

Constraint: format adherence must hold on long inputs too.

What is the correct prompt ordering fix?

choices.A: Put the examples in the middle of the user message.
choices.B: Shorten the user emails before sending them.
choices.C: Add more few-shot examples so some survive truncation.
choices.D: Move the task instructions and few-shot examples before the user content, since truncation removes content from the end of the context, not the beginning.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Truncation removes content from the end of the context. Instructions and examples placed first form a stable prefix. This prefix stays. If you place them after the user message, the system cuts them first on long inputs.
C is wrong. More examples after the user message are still after the truncation point. The system cuts them too.
A is wrong. Examples buried in the middle of a message are still downstream of long content. The system can cut or dilute them.
B is wrong. Shortening user emails removes the actual task input. This happens to protect the formatting.

question:
A support agent's system prompt has grown to 15,000 tokens. Three sections change daily (pricing, promos, policy updates). The rest is stable. The team enabled prompt caching, but the cache hit rate is near zero, because any daily change invalidates the whole cached prompt.

Constraint: maximize cache hits so the stable 12,000 tokens are not reprocessed on every request.

How do you restructure the prompt?

choices.A: Keep one prompt but enable caching twice, which doubles the hit rate.
choices.B: Split the prompt into modules. Put cache breakpoints between the modules. Order the modules stable-first. The stable base caches one time. Only the changed daily sections process again.
choices.C: Move the daily sections to the front. This processes them first.
choices.D: Remove the daily sections from the prompt and hope the model knows current pricing.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Cache breakpoints let each stable prefix cache independently. Order stable content first. The 12,000-token base hits the cache on every request. Only reprocess the small volatile modules when they change.
A is wrong. You cannot enable caching twice. One changing byte still invalidates one cached blob.
C is wrong. Putting volatile content first poisons the cache for everything after it. This includes the entire stable base.
D is wrong. Dropping pricing and policy from context guarantees wrong answers about pricing and policy.

question:
A code editor's autocomplete must respond in less than 300 milliseconds at p99. An engineer enabled extended thinking on the Sonnet model. This was "for better completions." P99 latency is now 2.1 seconds. Users complain.

Constraint: p99 latency under 300ms; completions only need the obvious next token, not deep reasoning.

What is the right change?

choices.A: Turn off extended thinking and use a fast model with a small max-tokens limit; match the effort setting to the task. Note that Haiku has no extended thinking at all, which tells you what it is for.
choices.B: Add a loading spinner so users tolerate the 2.1 seconds.
choices.C: Cache completions so thinking only runs once per prefix.
choices.D: Keep extended thinking but raise the thinking budget so the model finishes faster.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Extended thinking trades latency for reasoning depth. Autocomplete does not need this. Disabling it and using a fast model with tight output limits directly attacks the 300ms budget. The constraint is about effort matched to the task.
D is wrong. A larger thinking budget means more reasoning. This increases latency further. This is the opposite of the fix.
B is wrong. A spinner masks the symptom. The 2.1-second p99 still violates the constraint.
C is wrong. Caching prefixes helps only repeated prefixes. It leaves first-seen completions at 2.1 seconds.

question:
A team faces a one-off data migration: two days of work moving records between systems with custom rules. An engineer proposes packaging the whole procedure as a versioned Skill with documentation and review.

Constraint: do not over-invest in work that happens once.

What is the right call?

choices.A: Build the Skill but skip the documentation to save time.
choices.B: Build the versioned Skill. Skills are a good method.
choices.C: Use plain prompt text or a script for the one-off migration; Skills earn their keep on recurring workflows that need reuse, versioning, and maintenance.
choices.D: Skip the migration and keep both systems running.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Skills are useful through reuse. Versioning and maintenance are worth the effort when a workflow happens many times. For a one-time task, that investment is only overhead. Prompt text or a script does the job.
B is wrong because "best practice" without recurrence counts as over-engineering. The constraint explicitly bans over-investment here.
D is wrong. Avoiding the migration does not satisfy the business need. It avoids the question.
A is wrong. An undocumented Skill is worse than prompt text. It has maintenance cost. It has none of the reusability benefit.

question:
A logistics company needs live carrier data inside its Claude agent. The carrier exposes its data only through a proprietary Python SDK; there is no REST API and no documentation beyond the SDK. Three internal teams will need the same carrier data in their own agents.

Constraint: build the integration once and reuse it across all three teams, with the vendor's quirks isolated in one place.

Which integration approach fits?

choices.A: Have each team call the SDK directly from its own agent code.
choices.B: Wrap the SDK in a single MCP server with clean, well-named tools; all three teams use the server, and vendor quirks live behind its interface.
choices.C: Use an agent-to-agent protocol so the carrier's system negotiates directly with each agent.
choices.D: Ask the model to read the SDK source and call it ad hoc per request.

explanation:
Why B is correct: An MCP server built once gives every team the same clean tool interface. It isolates the proprietary SDK in exactly one place. That is the build-once rationale. There is one integration to maintain. There are three consumers.
A is wrong. Three direct integrations triple the maintenance surface. They spread vendor quirks across three codebases.
C is wrong. Agent-to-agent protocols connect agents to agents. The carrier exposes an SDK. It does not expose an agent.
D is wrong. Ad-hoc SDK calls per request are unreviewable. They are untestable. They reinvent the integration on every call.

question:
A finance agent got 23 tools. This included a raw SQL tool "for flexibility." Wrong-tool calls increase. The model picks similar tools. It then tries again. It once ran an unfiltered SELECT over the transactions table.

Constraint: keep every capability the agent needs, but cut wrong-tool calls and remove the dangerous flexibility.

What is the best fix?

choices.A: Consolidate into a few parameterized tools with narrow, well-named operations (for example, one reporting tool with explicit query types), and remove raw SQL entirely; review the catalog for overlap.
choices.B: Add a "tool recommender" tool that picks the right tool for each request.
choices.C: Document all 23 tools more thoroughly in the system prompt.
choices.D: Upgrade to a larger model that can distinguish 23 tools more reliably.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Fewer, distinct, well-named tools reduce the model's choice confusion. Removing raw SQL enforces least privilege structurally. Consolidation keeps the capabilities. It removes the misfire surface and the dangerous generality.
D is wrong. Tool-bloat is an architectural problem. It is not a capacity problem. A larger model still faces 23 similar choices.
B is wrong. A recommender adds a 24th tool. It adds another model judgment to the path that is already failing.
C is wrong. Longer descriptions do not fix overlapping, confusing tool boundaries. The catalog itself is the problem.

question:
A finance team wants to connect a third-party MCP server. This server files invoices. It starts payments. The server's tool descriptions are good. An engineer reviews the server. The server is closed-source.

The vendor hosts it. Its "initiate_payment" tool takes a free-text amount and recipient.

Constraint: no unauthorized money movement may be possible, even if the MCP server or its descriptions are malicious.

Which two controls satisfy the constraint? (Select two)

choices.A: Add "never initiate payments before the user asks two times" to the agent's system prompt.
choices.B: Validate every tool result and enforce payment authorization in your own code (the effect-performing layer), so a malicious or compromised description cannot trigger money movement by itself.
choices.C: Trust the tool descriptions and the vendor's SOC 2 report, and connect the server directly.
choices.D: Treat the server as untrusted. Pin a reviewed version of the server. Run it with least-privilege credentials. These credentials cannot move money alone. Require explicit human consent inside your system. Do this before any payment executes.

explanation:
Why D, B is correct: Trust boundaries must assume tool descriptions are text that attackers control. Least-privilege credentials and human consent stop the server from acting alone (D). Enforce authorization at the effect-performing layer. The payment decision never depends on the third party's words (B).
C is wrong. A SOC 2 report describes the vendor's controls. It does not describe the safety of granting its server payment power. Descriptions remain untrusted input.
A is wrong. A prompt instruction is bypassable. This is the prompt-plea trap. It guards money movement.

question:
A support RAG system served p99 retrieval latency of 400ms. After indexing a new set of 200-page PDF manuals, p99 spiked to 4 seconds. Queries are short ("reset procedure model X"); the new documents are long. Recall on the new manuals matters.

Constraint: bring p99 back under 800ms without losing recall on the new manuals.

Which two changes address the root cause? (Select two)

choices.A: Chunk the PDFs by document structure. Use sections and headings. Make small retrievable units. Do not make one chunk per document. Short queries match precise passages. The reranker has less to process.
choices.B: Add metadata filters (product model, document type) and a hybrid keyword-plus-vector search so short factual queries hit exact terms without scanning the whole index.
choices.C: Increase the top-k from 10 to 100 to improve recall.
choices.D: Upgrade to a larger embedding model for better semantic matches.

explanation:
Why A, B is correct: The spike comes from giant chunks. Long documents dilute matches. They also bloat reranking. Structure-aware small chunks restore precision for short queries (A). Metadata filters plus hybrid search cut the candidate set. This happens before the expensive steps.
This brings p99 down (B).
D is wrong. A larger embedding model increases per-query compute. It does nothing about the chunk-size mismatch. The failure is in chunking and index strategy. Embedding capacity is not the failure.
C is wrong. Raising top-k increases reranking work. It increases latency further. It treats a precision problem as a recall problem.

question:
A retailer classifies 2 million product descriptions every night. The job streams through the real-time API. It costs $4,800 per night. The retailer needs results by 6am. This is for the morning catalog build. No one looks at them before 6am.

Constraint: finish by 6am at the lowest cost; interactivity is worth nothing here.

Which API choice fits?

choices.A: Sample 10 percent of the descriptions to cut cost.
choices.B: Keep the real-time streaming API, since it finishes fastest.
choices.C: Move the job to the Batch API: roughly 50 percent cheaper with up to 24-hour turnaround, which easily covers an overnight deadline.
choices.D: Split the job across two streaming API keys to double throughput.

explanation:
Why C is correct: The Batch API trades latency for a roughly 50 percent discount. The job's only latency requirement is "by 6am." Paying real-time prices for results nobody reads until morning is waste.
B is wrong. "Fastest" buys nothing here. The catalog build reads the results at 6am regardless.
D is wrong. Two keys double throughput. The job does not need this. It keeps the expensive real-time price.
A is wrong. Sampling 10 percent silently drops 90 percent of the catalog. It cuts cost by cutting the work.

question:
An e-commerce agent answers "is this in stock?". A proposal will index the inventory database into the vector store. The system will refresh the vector store hourly. The agent can then answer from retrieval.

Constraint: the agent must never promise stock that is not actually there; an oversell means a refund and an angry customer.

Where should live inventory levels come from?

choices.A: The model's training knowledge of typical stock levels.
choices.B: The hourly vector index, since retrieval is fast.
choices.C: A direct tool call to the inventory system at decision time; the vector index holds stable knowledge, not mutable state.
choices.D: A twice-hourly vector index, which is fresher.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Inventory is a live state. It changes between any two index refreshes. Only a read at decision time shows the current reality. A vector index is for stable knowledge. A 30-minute-old snapshot can oversell.
B is wrong. An hourly snapshot is stale by definition. The system does not see items sold in the last hour.
D is wrong. Refreshing twice as often halves the staleness window. It keeps the structural flaw. It doubles the indexing cost.
A is wrong. Training knowledge is months old. It was never about this store's stock.

question:
A travel agent calls a partner airline API. The partner has degraded: responses now take 40 seconds. The agent waits, users time out, and the agent's retries pile more load onto the struggling partner.

Constraint: the agent must stay responsive even while the partner is slow, and must not make the partner's overload worse.

Which resilience design meets the constraint?

choices.A: Set a short timeout. Cap concurrent partner calls with a bulkhead. Trip a circuit breaker after repeated failures. Serve a graceful fallback. For example, show "live prices unavailable, showing cached fares". Do not let the system hang.
choices.B: Queue all partner requests and process them serially to be gentle.
choices.C: Remove the timeout entirely so slow responses can complete.
choices.D: Raise the retry budget and add exponential backoff so every request eventually succeeds.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Timeouts bound the wait. The bulkhead caps how much of the agent the partner can consume. The circuit breaker stops the retry pile-on. The fallback keeps the agent responsive. Each piece answers one half of the constraint.
D is wrong. More retries against a degraded partner is a retry storm. It deepens the overload. Users still wait.
B is wrong. A serial queue turns 40-second responses into unbounded user-facing latency. Gentleness to the partner is bought with the agent's responsiveness.
C is wrong. No timeout means one slow partner can hang the agent's workers indefinitely.

question:
A billing agent listens for payment webhooks. The provider's documents warn that the provider can deliver webhooks more than one time. Last month, a duplicate delivery charged a customer two times. The refund cost the company the customer.

Constraint: the charge must happen exactly once per triggering event, even if the webhook arrives five times.

Where must the system enforce idempotency? How must the system enforce idempotency?

choices.A: The payment service uses the webhook's event ID. The service checks the key before it charges. This stops duplicate charges.
choices.B: Ask the customer to confirm before each charge, which catches duplicates.
choices.C: Deduplicate in the webhook receiver's in-memory cache.
choices.D: In the agent's conversation memory: remember processed webhook IDs and skip repeats.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Idempotency must be at the effect-performing service. It uses the triggering event's ID. The payment service can guarantee exactly-once charging. This is true for restarts. This is true for retries. This is true for duplicate deliveries.
D is wrong. Conversation memory is per-session and ephemeral. A restart or a second agent instance forgets it. The double charge returns.
B is wrong. Customer confirmation is bad UX. It is still racy. The system must confirm two deliveries.
C is wrong. An in-memory cache dies with the process. Durability is the whole point of idempotency.

question:
A news summarizer's ROUGE score has sat at 0.41 for three months. Meanwhile support tickets complaining about bad summaries ("missed the key point", "invented a quote") have tripled. The team keeps tuning to hold ROUGE steady.

Constraint: the eval must measure what users actually experience, not what is easy to compute.

What should replace ROUGE as the primary quality signal?

choices.A: A larger eval set scored with ROUGE, for tighter confidence intervals.
choices.B: BLEU instead of ROUGE, for a second opinion.
choices.C: A higher ROUGE target, since the metric is standard.
choices.D: Human-judged evals on a sampled set of production summaries, scored on task-grounded criteria (key points present, no invented quotes), plus tracking the support-ticket themes as a metric.

explanation: Why D is correct: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap. This stopped tracking the failures users report. Human judges scoring task-grounded criteria measure the actual experience. Ticket themes turn user pain into a metric the team can move. C is wrong. Optimizing harder for a proxy that has decoupled from quality produces better-scoring bad summaries. A is wrong. A larger sample of the same proxy metric gives more confidence in the wrong number. B is wrong. BLEU is the same family of overlap proxy. Swapping proxies does not fix a proxy problem.

question:
A support bot's eval suite is from last quarter's tickets. It is fully green. But production quality is bad. The company launched a new product line two months ago. The bot does not answer questions about it well. The eval set has no tickets about the new line.

Constraint: evals must predict current production quality.

What is the fix?

choices.A: Tune the model until the old eval scores improve further.
choices.B: Wait a quarter so the new product's tickets age into the set naturally.
choices.C: Add more last-quarter tickets to the eval set for statistical power.
choices.D: Refresh the eval set. Make it match the current production mix. Stratify it by topic and recency. Include the new product line. Re-baseline scores on the refreshed set.

explanation: Why D is correct: An evaluation set measures the world it was drawn from. Production drifted. The set did not. Refreshing to the current mix makes the scores predictive again. The new line is explicitly covered. C is wrong. More old tickets add precision about a world that no longer exists. This is a stale-evaluation trap. A is wrong. Higher scores on a stale set prove nothing about the new product line's questions. B is wrong. Flying blind for a quarter is the exact cost the constraint wants to avoid.

question:
Two candidate prompts for invoice extraction tie on accuracy (96.2% vs 96.1% on the eval set). Prompt A costs $0.021 per document; Prompt B costs $0.007 per document. At 400,000 documents a month, the difference is real money.

Constraint: pick the cheaper prompt with no hidden regressions.

How should the architect decide?

choices.A: Pick the prompt with fewer tokens in the template, since that is simpler.
choices.B: Run both in production for a month and see which feels better.
choices.C: Pick Prompt A; 96.2 beats 96.1 and accuracy is king.
choices.D: Compare total cost per completed document (input plus output tokens, retries, tool calls), confirm the accuracy tie holds on a held-out set, check guardrail metrics (latency, format validity), then pick Prompt B.

explanation: Why D is correct: When accuracy ties, total cost per completed task is the tiebreaker. This is only after confirming the tie is real. Use a held-out set to confirm the tie. Confirm that no guardrail regressed. Every step guards one way the "cheaper" choice could be a mirage. C is wrong. A 0.1-point evaluation difference is noise. It costs three times the money for nothing measurable. A is wrong. Template token count ignores output tokens. It ignores retries and tool calls. This is where the real cost lives. B is wrong. "See which feels better" is not a measurement. It ships an undecided experiment to production.

question:
A team canaries a new model version at 5% of traffic. Quality looks slightly better, but the escalation-to-human rate wobbles: up 1.5 points in the first hour, flat in the second. The team argues in Slack about whether to roll back. Nobody wrote down what "bad enough to roll back" means.

Constraint: the rollback decision must be automatic, not a debate; the criteria must exist before the canary starts.

Which two practices satisfy the constraint? (Select two)

choices.A: Pre-register rollback triggers before the canary starts (for example, escalation rate up 2 points sustained 30 minutes), wired to automatic rollback; the debate happens once, at registration time.
choices.B: Let the on-call engineer decide based on experience during the canary.
choices.C: Watch the dashboard more closely during the canary, with two engineers on call.
choices.D: Define the primary metric. Define guardrail metrics. Define minimum runtime. Define minimum sample size. Do this before you start. This way, "wobbles" are not signal or noise later.

explanation: Why A, D is correct: Pre-registered triggers with automatic rollback remove the in-the-moment argument (A). Pre-defined metrics and minimum sample sizes stop the team. They stop the team from cherry-picking wobbles as wins or noise (D). Both move the judgment to before the experiment. This is where it belongs. B is wrong. On-call judgment during the incident is the debate. The constraint bans this debate. It also varies by who is on call. C is wrong. Closer watching improves observation. It does not improve decision-making. Two engineers can still disagree about the same dashboard.

question:
A team reports a 1% hallucination rate for its support agent, measured on its eval set. In production, hallucinations cluster on ambiguous, low-context questions ("it stopped working" with no product named), which make up 20% of traffic but only 2% of the eval set.

Constraint: know the true hallucination rate on the traffic that actually arrives.

How must you fix the eval?

choices.A: Report the 1% number with a footnote about the eval set composition.
choices.B: Stratify the eval set by query difficulty, oversample the known-hard tail (ambiguous, low-context queries), and report per-stratum rates weighted by the production mix.
choices.C: Remove the ambiguous queries from the eval set so the metric is clean.
choices.D: Test only on the easy queries but test more of them.

explanation: Why B is correct: The 1% headline is an aggregate. This aggregate uses the wrong mix. This is an aggregate trap. Stratifying and weighting by the production mix shows the true rate. This rate matters where failures are common. It shows the hard tail that causes most real failures. A is wrong. A footnote does not fix a misleading headline number. Decisions will still be made based on the 1% number. C is wrong. Deleting the hard cases makes a good metric. It hides the failures. D is wrong. More easy cases only re-measure what was already measured. The blind spot remains untouched.

question:
A growth team edits prompts directly in the production config. Twice this quarter a "small wording change" broke output formatting and took down a downstream parser. There is no record of what changed or when.

Constraint: no prompt change may reach production without proof it did not regress.

Which pipeline satisfies the constraint?

choices.A: Version prompts like code. Run the eval suite on every change in CI. Block the deploy on regression. Keep a changelog of what changed and why.
choices.B: Only allow prompt changes on Tuesdays, when the team is available to watch.
choices.C: Limit prompt edits to senior engineers, who make fewer mistakes.
choices.D: Require a second engineer to eyeball every prompt change before it ships.

explanation: Why A is correct: Versioning and eval-gated CI make "small wording change" a measured claim. The suite proves no regression. This happens before the deploy proceeds. The changelog makes every change attributable. D is wrong. Human eyeballing cannot reliably predict formatting regressions. It is review without measurement. B is wrong. A Tuesday deploy window changes when breakage happens. It does not change if breakage happens. C is wrong. Seniority reduces regressions. It does not eliminate them. It proves nothing about any specific change.
